case_study_insert.main_stem: Dunmore Plastics (DMP) is a private limited company in the agricultural plastics sector, extruding uPVC irrigation pipes and fittings for farm suppliers, employing a workforce of 81. Founded in 2010 by Daniel Soriano, the business operates a flat structure with laissez-faire leadership and is based in Cebu, the Philippines. DMP plans to invest $1,350,000 in a second uPVC extrusion line with in-line wall-thickness testing, financed by a $800,000 bank loan and $550,000 from the sale of its old delivery fleet. It has fixed costs of $315,000 a year, a variable cost of $8.10 a unit and a selling price of $12.60, and currently produces 110,000 units a year. DMP faces a serious quality problem: customer complaints about inconsistent pipe wall thickness rose for two consecutive quarters.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Market Research Summary — Q3 2025: The extrusion line produced 27,000 units last quarter at a defect rate of 2.8%, down from 4.2% a year ago. Customer complaints about pipe wall thickness fell from 19 to 10 per month. Average order fulfilment is 2.6 days. DMP is trialling 30% recycled uPVC regrind in non-pressure pipe grades, with early trials showing 15% lower resin cost per metre. A market research survey of 280 farm supply managers found that 69% would switch suppliers for certified wall-thickness consistency and 45% would accept a 4% price premium for UV-stabilised uPVC pipe. Off-the-job courses at the local college cost $500 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Dunmore Plastics as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.75% to 5.50%, the fourth rise this year, increasing repayment costs on variable-rate business loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.4% from $10.90 to $11.60 per hour from April 2026, raising wage bills across manufacturing. (3) uPVC resin and stabiliser input costs have risen 11.2% year-on-year, industrial inflation is running at 7.1%, and agricultural output grew 3.1% in the same period.

questions.question_text: DMP plans to finance part of its extrusion-line expansion from the sale of its old delivery fleet. Explain two advantages for DMP of using the sale of assets instead of relying entirely on the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Selling the old delivery fleet converts idle capital into $550,000 of usable funds without adding a single dollar of new debt to the $800,000 bank loan, so DMP's total obligations stay lower and its fixed charges of $315,000 a year are not inflated by extra interest. The fleet had reached the end of its economic life, so the sale releases trapped value at little operational cost while the new line is commissioned.

Point 2: Using asset sale proceeds avoids diluting ownership and avoids additional loan conditions or security demands on the new in-line wall-thickness testing equipment. It also simplifies the balance sheet ahead of any future audit of pipe consistency certificates for farm suppliers, demonstrates to lenders that DMP funds expansion from its own resources, and preserves headroom on the $1,350,000 programme should dealerships for the extrusion line run over budget.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Dunmore Plastics and its expansion decision.

questions.question_text: DMP is launching its certified wall-thickness consistent uPVC pipe range. Consider advertising in farm trade magazines, a presence at national agricultural shows, or Facebook and YouTube marketing aimed at farm suppliers. Which should DMP choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Farm trade magazine advertising: Full-page adverts in irrigation and farm-supply magazines reach professional buyers with long shelf life, technicians and owners can keep the certification details beside the catalogue, and the audience is directly the 280 farm supply managers DMP surveyed. Drawbacks are slow lead times, modest measurability, and wastage where circulation extends well beyond DMP's distributor patch in Cebu and the central Visayas.

National agricultural shows: A stand at the flagship farm show would let DMP demonstrate actual pipe cross-sections, wall-thickness certificates and the 4% UV-stabilised premium story face to face, and could sign up whole supplier networks in two days. The downsides are heavy fees, freight and staffing costs, a single-event impact window, and disruption to a lean 81-employee team during harvest-season demand peaks.

Facebook and YouTube marketing: Video demos of the in-line testing rig, customer testimonials from Cebu farm suppliers and reinforced UV-stabilised messaging target exactly the 69% who would switch for certified consistency and the 45% paying a 4% premium. Production is modest in cost, click-through and enquiry metrics are immediate, and content can be boosted to province-level farm-supply audiences — though creative quality drives results and younger followers may not match the buyer profile of every supply shop.

Recommendation: DMP should choose Facebook and YouTube marketing aimed at farm suppliers. It is cheap, measurable and precisely matched to the 69% switching segment and the 45% premium-accepting segment in its research, and it scales beyond any single show. Farm trade magazines are rejected as too slow and hard to measure for a first-mover range; the agricultural show is rejected as high fixed cost and short-lived for a small private limited company; social video should be supported by sending QR-linked certificate samples to every enquiring supplier to convert attention into trials.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of DMP with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of DMP with a well-justified recommendation explaining why trade magazines and the agricultural show are rejected.

questions.question_text: DMP's pipe wall-thickness complaints rose for two consecutive quarters. Explain two benefits for DMP of introducing job enrichment for its extrusion-line operators.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Job enrichment gives operators ownership of the full extrusion task — from resin feed through in-line wall-thickness checks to end-of-line certification — rather than minding a single machine. Operators who see the pipe leave the line certified are more invested in consistency, which directly attacks the two quarters of rising complaints and supports the 2.8% defect rate that has already improved from 4.2% a year ago.

Point 2: Enriched roles stretch skills and create the pipeline of certified in-line testers DMP needs for the new line, reducing dependence on Daniel Soriano's personal oversight. Higher responsibility satisfies the esteem needs (Maslow) and motivators (Herzberg) that pay alone cannot, raising attendance and lowering the monotony that long extrusion shifts create — protecting the 2.6-day fulfilment promise and helping DMP meet the 69% of farm supply managers ready to switch for certified consistency.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to DMP's quality problem, certification appeal and fulfilment record.

questions.question_text: DMP must fix rising wall-thickness complaints on the extrusion line. Consider installing the in-line CAM wall-thickness scanner operated by existing staff or hiring two full-time quality inspectors. Which should DMP choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
In-line CAM wall-thickness scanner: Computer-aided manufacturing scanning within the extruder feedback loop would measure every metre of pipe continuously, catch deviations before scrap is cut, and generate certificates farm suppliers can file. CAM is squarely within proven manufacturing technology and matches the $1,350,000 expansion's in-line theme. Limits: it needs calibration discipline, operators trained to respond to alarms (not just watch dashboards), and a real investment beyond the base line — plus residual dependence on the system vendor for maintenance.

Two full-time quality inspectors: Two inspectors would provide independent eyes, immediate physical checks at the end of line, and human judgement on borderline pipes. They also give DMP a visible commitment to farm suppliers who visit the works. The drawbacks are ongoing wages on top of a workforce of 81 and fixed costs of $315,000 a year, subjectivity and sampling gaps (however good, they cannot measure every metre), slower root-cause feedback because inspectors find defects after extrusion rather than during it, and no automatic certificate generation.

Decision: DMP should install the in-line CAM wall-thickness scanner and train existing operators to run it, backed by one senior inspector for periodic audits rather than two. The scanner prevents defects at the point of manufacture — exactly what the two consecutive quarters of complaints demand — certifies every metre for the 69% of managers ready to switch, and scales with the new line without growing payroll. Two full-time inspectors are rejected as a slower, costlier, sampling-based patch that finds rather than prevents wall-thickness drift; the single senior auditor keeps human judgement in the system while the scanner does the continuous measuring.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two quality approaches with limited application to DMP.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the advantages and disadvantages of one or both approaches in the context of DMP.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both approaches in the context of DMP with a well-justified decision covering prevention, cost, certification and inspection reach.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how DMP's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $12.60 − $8.10 = $4.50. Answer: contribution per unit is $4.50.

Formula: Margin of safety = Actual output − Break-even output. Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit = $315,000 ÷ $4.50 = 70,000 units. Substitution: 110,000 units − 70,000 units = 40,000 units. Answer: margin of safety is 40,000 units a year.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways DMP's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Managers can compare the 70,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 110,000 units to confirm the pipe line is comfortably profitable, with a margin of safety of 40,000 units, and use that headroom to schedule the new extrusion line's ramp-up without panic discounting.
2. Contribution per unit of $4.50 lets DMP model the 4% premium the 45% of managers will pay for UV-stabilised pipe, lifting the price to $13.10, letting managers judge whether resin renegotiation amid the 11.2% input-cost rise is still needed to hold margins.
3. Knowing fixed costs of $315,000 and contribution per unit helps managers test whether cash flow can service the $800,000 bank loan instalments before the second line reaches full capacity, and whether the $550,000 fleet sale proceeds cover fit-out without overdrawing.
4. Managers can use unit cost data ($315,000 ÷ 110,000 units + $8.10 = $10.96 a unit) to benchmark quarter against quarter, pinpoint waste behind the 2.8% defect rate, and evaluate whether the 30% recycled uPVC regrind trial and its 15% resin cost saving feed through to a stronger contribution per unit.

questions.model_answer: (i) Contribution per unit = $4.50 | (ii) margin of safety = 40,000 units | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: the 40,000-unit cushion against 110,000-unit output; pricing the 4% premium at $13.10; servicing the $800,000 bank loan with $315,000 fixed costs; and unit-cost benchmarking at $10.96 to test the recycled-regrind saving against the 2.8% defect rate.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate DMP's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has DMP's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.50 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.60 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.94 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.02 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $180,000 inventories + $235,000 trade receivables + $65,000 cash = $480,000; 2025 current assets = $190,000 + $255,000 + $75,000 = $520,000. 2024 = $480,000 ÷ $320,000 = 1.50; 2025 = $520,000 ÷ $325,000 = 1.60. Quick cover 2024 = ($480,000 − $180,000) ÷ $320,000 = $300,000 ÷ $320,000 = 0.94; 2025 = ($520,000 − $190,000) ÷ $325,000 = $330,000 ÷ $325,000 = 1.02.

Evaluation: Liquidity has improved and crossed an important threshold. Short-term cover rose from 1.50 to 1.60 and quick cover moved from 0.94 to 1.02 — DMP no longer needs to sell pipe inventory to meet every short-term bill, though only just. Cash improved from $65,000 to $75,000 and inventories are well controlled at $190,000, crucial for a business whose wall-thickness consistency drives its order book. The caution is liabilities rising only $5,000 while receivables rose $20,000 — DMP is underwriting its expansion increasingly from patient farm-supplier credit. Non-current assets grew from $2,050,000 to $2,600,000, so the enlarged base must now earn its keep; capital employed of $2,850,000 against operating risk in a niche pipe market deserves close monitoring.

Conclusion: DMP's financial position has improved. Short-term cover (1.50 to 1.60) and quick cover (0.94 to 1.02) show stronger short-term solvency, and the quick-cover move above 1.0 means inventory is no longer the primary defence against short-term demands. Residual risks are the $20,000 receivables rise and the heavier asset base post-expansion, so DMP should tighten supplier payment terms, keep the certified-pipe premium pricing intact, and ensure the new line's CAM system is online before further capacity is committed.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables, cash and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether DMP's financial position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for DMP of using 30% recycled uPVC regrind in its irrigation pipes.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Using 30% recycled regrind directly supports DMP's trial results showing 15% lower resin cost per metre, helping absorb the 11.2% uPVC resin and stabiliser inflation while protecting the $4.50 contribution per unit. It also gives farm supply managers a credible sustainability story to pair with the UV-stabilised premium — the 45% willing to pay 4% more get real environmental content, and DMP can position itself as the low-waste pipe brand ahead of competitors who still sell virgin resin only.

Disadvantage: Recycled content can introduce variability in melt flow and colour consistency, which risks undoing the certified wall-thickness consistency that 69% of switchers demand. If non-pressure grade pipes perform poorly in real irrigation conditions — embrittlement, joint leaks, UV-degradation faster than lab tests suggest — complaints will rise again just as DMP is commissioning a second line, and the 15% resin saving will be wiped out by returns, rework and lost trust among supply shops that switched fleets for DMP certificates.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to DMP's trials, research data, costs and certification positioning.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.50%, the 6.4% minimum wage increase and the 11.2% rise in input costs will affect DMP. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.75% to 5.50%): If DMP's $800,000 ten-year bank loan is variable, the 0.75 percentage point rise adds 0.75% × $800,000 = $6,000 a year (0.0075 × $800,000) to interest costs — noticeable against fixed costs of $315,000 a year, and zero if the loan was fixed at signing. The risk extends to any future borrowing for the remaining kit on the $1,350,000 programme and to farm suppliers slowing their own capital spending, though higher rates can also cool rival imports. DMP should confirm its loan rate and consider partial early repayment from operating cash before expansion peak.

Minimum wage increase (6.4%, to $11.60 per hour from April 2026): With 81 staff mostly on hourly extrusion and packing rates, the rise is unavoidable. The insert gives no hours or pay split, so no annual wage total can be honestly invented; the honest benchmark is productivity: 110,000 units ÷ 81 staff ≈ 1,358 units per worker a year. If the new line lifts this figure, the rise is absorbable; if commissioning drags, unit labour cost climbs, the $4.50 contribution shrinks, and DMP's ability to service the $550,000 of asset-sale-funded expansion weakens precisely when overtime demand is peaking.

Input cost inflation (11.2% uPVC resin and stabilisers): DMP's $8.10 variable cost is dominated by raw resin, but the insert never decomposes it, so only an illustrative bound is defensible: if the whole variable cost rose 11.2% it would add 11.2% × $8.10 = $0.91 per unit (0.112 × $8.10 = $0.907); at 110,000 units a year that is about $99,792 (0.112 × $8.10 × 110,000). Even a milder illustrative $0.60 per unit strips roughly $66,000 a year. The 30% recycled regrind trial (15% lower resin cost per metre) helps, but stabiliser costs also rise 11.2%, and stabiliser performance is exactly what the UV-stabilised premium depends on.

Conclusion: The 11.2% rise in input costs will have the greatest impact. It multiplies across all 110,000 units, compresses the $4.50 contribution from both ends, and cannot be fixed by refinancing — only by pricing, renegotiation and the regrind programme. The minimum wage rise is second, absorbable if the new line raises productivity beyond roughly 1,358 units per worker; the interest rate rise is third at about $6,000 a year on a variable $800,000 loan. DMP should lock resin and stabiliser contracts through 2027, hold the 4% premium fiercely, and use agricultural output growth of 3.1% to win certified-pipe share before inflation compounds further.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to DMP.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on DMP's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of DMP with a well-justified judgment that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
